title: Infectious Endocrine Diseases
subject: Endocrine System (ENDO)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers two infections that strike an endocrine gland directly. Acute suppurative thyroiditis is a rare, focal bacterial infection of the thyroid that usually leaves hormone levels normal, and its main danger is abscess and spread through the neck. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral adrenal hemorrhage during overwhelming sepsis, classically meningococcemia, in which DIC destroys both adrenals and adds acute adrenal insufficiency to septic shock. Board questions usually give a febrile patient with a painful thyroid or a spreading purpuric rash with refractory hypotension and ask you to name the process, explain a finding, or separate it from a look-alike. Both are solved by reasoning from anatomy and mechanism.
prerequisites: Thyroid anatomy, follicle structure, and hormone storage as colloid
Pharyngeal pouch derivatives and the embryology of the neck
Adrenal cortex zones, cortisol and aldosterone actions, and the HPA axis
Coagulation cascade, protein C pathway, and fibrinolysis
Neisseria meningitidis structure and virulence factors (EN-11)

connections.how: The organisms, virulence factors, and pyriform sinus fistula anatomy behind both diseases are taught there in microbiologic detail.
Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is the main painful look-alike of bacterial thyroiditis and is separated from it by thyroid function and uptake.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is one cause of the adrenal crisis described there, and Sheehan syndrome is its pituitary counterpart.
The DIC that drives the rash and the adrenal hemorrhage follows the same consumption pattern seen in every other cause of DIC.
The same organism causes meningococcal meningitis, but fulminant septicemia with adrenal hemorrhage can occur without meningitis.

terms.def: Bacterial, pus-forming infection of the thyroid, usually confined to one lobe.
A persistent tract from the apex of the pyriform sinus to the thyroid region, a remnant of a caudal pharyngeal pouch, nearly always on the left.
A localized collection of pus in a cavity formed when neutrophil enzymes liquefy infected tissue.
A region of a thyroid scan that takes up little or no radioiodine because it contains no functioning follicles.
Hemorrhagic destruction of both adrenal glands during overwhelming sepsis, causing acute primary adrenal insufficiency.
Bloodstream infection with Neisseria meningitidis, which may occur with or without meningitis.
Widespread activation of coagulation that forms microthrombi and consumes platelets and clotting factors, so thrombosis and bleeding occur together.
Rapidly spreading hemorrhagic skin necrosis caused by thrombosis of dermal vessels, often with acquired protein C deficiency.
Cortisol's support of the vascular response to catecholamines and angiotensin II, without which vessels respond poorly to pressor signals.
Life-threatening acute adrenal insufficiency with hypotension, hypoglycemia, and electrolyte disturbance.

blocks.text: Acute suppurative thyroiditis is a bacterial infection of the thyroid that forms pus. It is rare because the gland resists infection: it is encapsulated, has a rich blood supply and lymphatic drainage, and its follicles contain iodine and generate hydrogen peroxide for hormone synthesis. Infection therefore needs either a direct route into the gland or a weakened gland.

In children the usual route is a pyriform sinus fistula, a remnant of a caudal pharyngeal pouch that runs from the pharynx to the left lobe, so infections are left-sided and recur while the tract persists. In adults the gland is more often seeded through the blood or by direct spread in someone with nodular goiter, thyroid cancer, recent needle aspiration, or immunosuppression. The organisms are those of skin and upper airway: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and mixed oropharyngeal anaerobes when a fistula is present. Immunocompromised hosts can also develop fungal or mycobacterial infection (EN-11).

blocks.title: From pyriform sinus fistula to thyroid abscess
steps: Pharyngeal pouch remnant persists, usually on the left
Upper respiratory infection inflames the pharynx
Oropharyngeal bacteria travel down the tract
Neutrophil enzymes liquefy tissue into an abscess
Pus can track into deep neck spaces
blocks.caption: Infection stays focal in one lobe, which is why hormone levels usually stay normal.

blocks.text: Each finding follows from focal bacterial inflammation. IL-1 and IL-6 raise the hypothalamic set point, giving fever above 38 °C (100.4 °F), often with chills. One lobe becomes swollen, warm, red, and very tender, with pain that may radiate to the ear or jaw; swallowing hurts because the gland moves with the larynx. Fluctuance means liquefied pus. Blood tests show neutrophilic leukocytosis and raised ESR and CRP. TSH and free T4 are usually normal because most follicles are untouched; occasionally follicle destruction releases enough stored hormone for transient thyrotoxicosis, and extensive destruction (more often in fungal disease) can cause hypothyroidism. Ultrasound shows the abscess, and needle aspiration yields neutrophils and organisms on Gram stain and culture. The abscess takes up no radioiodine, so it is a cold area while the rest of the gland is normal.

blocks.title: Painful thyroid: bacterial versus subacute granulomatous thyroiditis
rows: One lobe, warm, red, may be fluctuant
blocks.caption: Normal hormone levels with a hot, focal, fluctuant lobe point to infection.

blocks.text: Abscess is the key complication. Pus can rupture into the parapharyngeal, retropharyngeal, or prevertebral spaces and descend into the mediastinum, swelling can compress the trachea, and inflammation near the recurrent laryngeal nerve can cause hoarseness. Bacteremia can lead to sepsis.

blocks.title: Reading a painful thyroid
blocks.text: An 8-year-old has fever of 39 °C (102.2 °F) and a red, tender left neck swelling a week after a cold; it is his second episode. TSH and free T4 are normal and WBC is high. Normal hormone levels argue against a diffuse destructive process such as subacute thyroiditis, which would release stored hormone. A recurrent, left-sided infection after an upper respiratory infection points to a pyriform sinus fistula carrying pharyngeal bacteria to the left lobe. A fluctuant area on examination or a fluid collection on ultrasound means an abscess has formed.

blocks.predict: Why do most patients with bacterial thyroiditis stay euthyroid while patients with subacute thyroiditis become thyrotoxic?
blocks.explain: Bacterial infection destroys a limited region, so most follicles keep storing and releasing hormone normally. Subacute thyroiditis inflames the whole gland and breaks many follicles at once, releasing stored T4 and T3 while uptake falls.

blocks.text: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is massive hemorrhage into both adrenal glands during overwhelming sepsis. At autopsy both glands are enlarged sacs of clotted blood with cortical necrosis. Neisseria meningitidis is the classic cause; Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Staphylococcus aureus cause it less often. Risk follows the risk of meningococcemia: children and young adults, crowded living, asplenia, and deficiency of terminal complement (C5 to C9) or properdin.

Meningococci continually shed outer membrane blebs rich in lipooligosaccharide (endotoxin). Its lipid A activates TLR4 on monocytes and endothelium, releasing TNF, IL-1, and IL-6. These cytokines induce tissue factor and suppress thrombomodulin and the protein C pathway, so coagulation is switched on throughout the microcirculation and DIC develops. The adrenal is thought to be vulnerable because of its vascular design: many small arteries feed a subcapsular plexus and sinusoids, but all blood leaves through a single central vein. Thrombosis of that outflow while arterial inflow continues, plus damaged capillaries, causes hemorrhagic infarction of both glands. The exact trigger is not fully settled.

blocks.title: Meningococcemia to adrenal hemorrhage
steps: Meningococci multiply in blood and shed endotoxin
Lipid A activates TLR4; TNF and IL-1 released
Tissue factor up, protein C pathway down
DIC: microthrombi, platelets and factors consumed
Adrenal venous outflow clots; sinusoids rupture
Both adrenals infarct: cortisol and aldosterone lost
blocks.caption: The same DIC that destroys the adrenals produces the skin rash.

blocks.text: The rash comes from the same process. Microthrombi and endothelial injury in dermal vessels let red cells leak, giving nonblanching petechiae on the trunk and legs that enlarge within hours into purpura; with acquired protein C deficiency, skin and digits can necrose (purpura fulminans). Shock has several causes. Cytokines dilate vessels, open capillary leak, and depress the myocardium. Loss of cortisol then removes its permissive support of vascular tone, so vessels respond poorly to catecholamines and fluids, and loss of aldosterone adds sodium and water wasting. Cortisol loss also removes gluconeogenic support, so hypoglycemia is common. Because the onset is abrupt, ACTH has no time to cause hyperpigmentation.

blocks.title: Why the shock becomes refractory
steps: Hypoperfusion and acidosis worsen endothelial injury
Cortisol loss blunts response to catecholamines
blocks.caption: Each turn of the loop removes more of the body's compensation.

blocks.title: Findings and their mechanisms
rows: Low platelets, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer
Consumption in DIC with secondary fibrinolysis
Aldosterone loss (primary failure); sepsis acidosis and kidney injury also raise K+
Low or inappropriately normal cortisol with high ACTH
Fulminant septicemia can kill before meningitis develops
blocks.caption: Electrolyte changes may be absent early because the course is so fast.

blocks.text: Two distinctions are tested. Sheehan syndrome is pituitary necrosis, so adrenal insufficiency is secondary: aldosterone, controlled mainly by angiotensin II and potassium, is preserved, so hyperkalemia does not occur, although cortisol deficiency can still cause hyponatremia. Chronic Addison disease develops over months with hyperpigmentation, whereas Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome develops over hours. Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage also occurs without sepsis in anticoagulation, antiphospholipid syndrome, and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

blocks.predict: A septic patient with spreading purpura stays hypotensive despite fluids and catecholamines. Which hormone loss best explains the poor vascular response, and why?
blocks.explain: Loss of cortisol. Cortisol is permissive for vascular reactivity: it supports adrenergic receptor responsiveness and the vessel's response to catecholamines and angiotensin II, so without it pressor signals produce little vasoconstriction. Aldosterone loss adds volume depletion.
blocks.check: The shock paragraph and the refractory shock cycle.

integration.text: Both diseases are explained by anatomy. An embryologic remnant, the pyriform sinus fistula, gives bacteria a path into a gland that otherwise resists infection, and the adrenal's rich arterial inflow with a single draining vein makes it the endocrine organ that bleeds when DIC clots small veins. Microbiology and immunology supply the trigger: skin and pharyngeal flora in the thyroid, and in the adrenal a heavily encapsulated, endotoxin-shedding diplococcus normally cleared by complement and the spleen.

Physiology explains the findings. Focal thyroid infection spares enough follicles to keep hormone levels normal, while sudden loss of cortisol and aldosterone turns septic shock into shock that resists fluids and pressors. How much adrenal hemorrhage causes the shock, rather than marking its severity, is still debated.

summary: The thyroid resists infection because of its capsule, rich blood and lymph flow, and iodide and hydrogen peroxide in its follicles.
Acute suppurative thyroiditis needs a route or a weakened gland: a left pyriform sinus fistula in children, or nodular goiter, aspiration, or immunosuppression in adults.
It presents with fever and one hot, tender, sometimes fluctuant lobe; thyroid function is usually normal because most follicles are spared.
Abscess is the main complication and can spread to deep neck spaces and mediastinum or compress the airway.
Subacute thyroiditis differs: postviral, diffusely tender, thyrotoxic, with low uptake and granulomas.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral adrenal hemorrhage in overwhelming sepsis, classically meningococcemia with DIC.
Endotoxin drives cytokines, tissue factor, and protein C loss; DIC clots the single adrenal vein and infarcts both glands.
Petechiae and purpura come from dermal microthrombi; refractory shock, hypoglycemia, and hyponatremia with hyperkalemia come from cortisol and aldosterone loss.
Unlike Sheehan syndrome, it is primary adrenal failure, so aldosterone is lost; unlike chronic Addison disease, there is no time for hyperpigmentation.

verify: The embryologic origin of the pyriform sinus fistula is given as the third pouch, the fourth pouch, or both, and the left-sided share is quoted from about 80 to over 90 percent; confirm the wording NABNE expects.
How often suppurative thyroiditis causes transient thyrotoxicosis or hypothyroidism varies widely between case series; the chapter states only that most patients are euthyroid.
The vascular explanation for adrenal hemorrhage (single central vein outflow) is the common teaching, but Robbins describes the mechanism as uncertain.
Whether adrenal hemorrhage causes or mainly marks the shock in Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is debated; confirm how NABNE frames it.
Cortisol cutoffs used to define adrenal insufficiency in critical illness differ between guidelines, so no number is given here.
Confirm whether NABNE uses the eponym Waterhouse-Friderichsen or the descriptive name bilateral adrenal hemorrhage.

A diagram of adrenal arterial supply and single venous drainage (adrenal-vasculature) and of the neck with a pyriform sinus fistula (pyriform-fistula) would help this chapter; requested for a future revision.
